title: Data into a job and back
sub: A job works on a copy: what you can put in it and how to get the result out
cards/0/title: A job gets a copy of its struct
cards/0/body:
A job struct is a parcel of data for another thread. On Schedule() the job system copies it byte by byte, and Execute runs on that copy. Whatever the job writes to its plain fields stays in the copy, so after Complete() your original job variable is unchanged.

The same goes for Run(): the extension method takes the struct by value, so it works on a copy too.

This is the first data question in an interview: “why is the job’s field still zero after Complete()?” Because the job never wrote to your struct.
cards/1/q: You replaced job.Schedule().Complete() with job.Run(). What does Debug.Log(job.sum) print now?
cards/1/options/0: 0: Run() gets a copy of the struct too
cards/1/options/1: The sum: Run() executes the job on the same thread
cards/1/options/3: Garbage: the field is not initialized
cards/1/explain: Run() is an extension method, and the struct is passed to it by value. Same thread, but still its own copy, and the sum stays there. The thread does not matter; what matters is where the job writes.
cards/1/wrong/1: Same thread, but the data is a copy: the extension method takes the struct by value.
cards/1/wrong/2: This is neither a race nor access to a busy container. There is no error, only a lost result.
cards/1/wrong/3: C# struct fields are always initialized: sum = 0, and it stays that way.
cards/2/title: Only blittable data in a job
cards/2/body:
Since the struct is copied byte by byte, it cannot hold references into the managed heap: a copied reference would point to an object the garbage collector may move and another thread may change. The docs say a job can only access blittable types. In practice the rule is unmanaged fields, no reference types. bool is not strictly blittable, but it works in jobs.

Allowed: numbers, Unity.Mathematics vectors, your own structs made of them, FixedString64Bytes and the other FixedString types, Native containers. Not allowed: T[], string, List<T>, classes, Transform and any UnityEngine object — Schedule() throws, and Burst will not compile such code.

A separate trap is mutable static fields. Nothing stops a non-Burst job from using them, but nothing protects them either: the docs warn plainly that it may crash your application. Burst rejects writes to statics, except through SharedStatic<T>.
cards/3/q: Which fields can go into a job struct? Pick all that apply.
cards/3/explain: Native containers, numbers and FixedString are unmanaged and can be copied byte by byte. string, int[] and GameObject are references into the managed heap: Schedule() throws, and Burst will not compile it.
cards/4/body:
A Native container in a struct is a small struct holding a pointer to native memory. Copying the job copies the pointer, not the data, so the copy and the original look at the same memory. The docs say it directly: after the job finishes, only data written to a NativeContainer is accessible.

For a single value people used to take a NativeArray of length 1 — the manual’s example still does. Collections has NativeReference<T> for that: one value, a .Value property, clearer to read.

The order is always the same: allocate → pass to the job → Complete() → read → Dispose(). Allocator.TempJob is for data that lives up to a few frames; allocators get their own lesson in this unit.

A habit: accumulate in a local variable and write .Value once at the end. It reads better, and you do not depend on the compiler figuring out it can keep the sum in a register.
cards/4/deep: Inside a NativeArray<T> are a pointer, a length, an allocator and, in the Editor, a few safety system fields. Copying the job copies those few fields, so scheduling is cheap however many elements the array has.
cards/5/body:
By default a container field in a job counts as read and write. To the safety system that job is a writer, and no other job may touch the container until the first one is done.

[ReadOnly] is a promise to only read. Per the docs it allows two jobs to run in parallel and read the same container. Writing to a [ReadOnly] container throws in the Editor.

[WriteOnly] means write only; reading such a container also throws in the Editor.

The rule: mark everything a job only reads as [ReadOnly]. It is the cheapest way to let the scheduler run jobs in parallel. And remember it is a promise checked only in the Editor; in a build it does not make the data immutable.
cards/6/q: Build a job that counts positive ids and returns the number through a container
cards/6/explain: The job only reads ids — [ReadOnly]. One number comes back through a NativeReference<int>, written to count.Value. NativeArray has no Value property, and [WriteOnly] on ids would break the reads.
cards/7/q: Which line throws in the Editor?
cards/7/explain: hp is marked [ReadOnly], but the job writes to it. In the Editor a write to a [ReadOnly] container is caught with an exception. Remove the attribute from hp: the job both reads and writes it.
cards/8/q: Two jobs read positions, but neither marks it [ReadOnly]. They are scheduled with no dependency on each other. What happens in the Editor?
cards/8/options/0: An exception on the second Schedule: without [ReadOnly] both count as writers
cards/8/options/2: The second job automatically waits for the first
cards/8/options/3: An exception in Execute when the second job reads positions
cards/8/explain: The safety system does not look at what a job actually does — it looks at the declarations. A field without [ReadOnly] is write access, and two independent writers of one container are caught as soon as the second is scheduled. Mark positions [ReadOnly] in both jobs and they run in parallel.
cards/8/wrong/1: The safety system judges by declarations, not by the code in Execute. Without [ReadOnly] the field is write access.
cards/8/wrong/2: The job system never adds dependencies on its own: you pass them explicitly, or you get an exception.
cards/8/wrong/3: The conflict is caught earlier, when the second job is scheduled, before it starts running.
cards/9/task: Fix Stats.Sum: the sum is always 0. In SumJob replace the float sum field with NativeReference<float> result, mark input [ReadOnly] and write the sum to result.Value. In Sum create result with Allocator.TempJob, after Complete() store result.Value in a local variable, dispose of result and return the sum.
cards/9/checks/3/label: SumJob has no plain float field for the result
cards/9/checks/4/label: The NativeReference is created with Allocator.TempJob
cards/9/checks/5/label: After Complete(), .Value is read into a variable, then Dispose() is called
cards/9/explain: The job writes to native memory that both the copy and the original NativeReference point to, so after Complete() the value is visible to the main thread. Read first, then Dispose(): after disposal you may not read .Value. In an interview: “a job gets a copy of its struct; results come back only through a container — for a single value, a NativeReference.”
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “Why can’t you return a result through a plain job field, while a NativeArray works?”
cards/10/options/0: Schedule copies the struct; a copy of a container is the same pointer to native memory, so writes through it are visible after Complete()
cards/10/options/1: NativeArray is a class, so it is passed by reference
cards/10/options/2: Fields are copied back only for jobs without Burst
cards/10/options/3: A field works too if you call Run() instead of Schedule()
cards/10/explain: The short answer: the job is a copy, a container is a pointer. Both get copied, but a copied pointer leads to the same memory. That is why a job’s output is always a container: NativeArray, NativeReference and the rest.
cards/10/wrong/1: NativeArray is a struct. The copies share memory because there is a pointer inside.
cards/10/wrong/2: Burst has nothing to do with it: fields are never copied back.
cards/10/wrong/3: Run() takes the struct by value as well.
